title: Edinburgh rock
subtitle: Scottish pastel sugar candy sticks
excerpt: Edinburgh rock is a distinctive Scottish confection, chalk-soft, crumbly rather than chewy, and pastel-coloured in flavours like raspberry, lemon, violet, and vanilla. It differs from the hard seaside rock of English coastal towns: the pulling process while the sugar is cooling creates a crystalline interior structure that dissolves on the tongue. This is pure sugar work and takes patience and timing, but the result is unlike anything shop-bought.
sourceNotes: Edinburgh rock was created in the early 19th century, traditionally attributed to a Glaswegian confectioner named Alexander Ferguson who set up shop in Edinburgh, earning the nickname 'Sweetie Sandy'. The candy became a Scottish souvenir staple and remains one of the most distinctive British regional confections. The key technical difference from other pulled sugar candies is that Edinburgh rock is 'worked' at a lower temperature (around 60°C) and then rested, allowing the sugar to crystallise over hours, this produces the powdery, crumbly texture rather than the glassy, hard texture of barley sugar or seaside rock.

recipe.batchNotes: Keeps in an airtight tin for up to 3 months. Best stored with a layer of icing sugar to prevent sticking.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make at least 12 hours before serving; the rock needs overnight to complete the crystallisation process.
recipe.temperatureNote: soft-crack stage for working; the pulling stage requires the sugar to be at about 60°C

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: soft-crack stage (127°C); the candy is worked (pulled) at about 60°C while still pliable, before it becomes too rigid to stretch

content.text: Edinburgh rock is a soft, crumbly, pastel-coloured sugar candy that dissolves on the tongue rather than snapping or chewing. It gets its texture from being pulled repeatedly while cooling, which creates a fine crystalline structure. If hot sugar touches skin, run cold water over it for at least ten minutes and seek medical care if needed. The timing is everything here: work the sugar too early and it won't hold shape; too late and it's too stiff to pull.

Combine the sugar, water, and cream of tartar in a medium saucepan. Heat gently, stirring, until the sugar dissolves. Bring to a boil without stirring. Cook to 127°C on a probe thermometer, the soft-crack stage. Add the food colouring and flavouring at this point, swirling the pan rather than stirring. Pour the syrup onto a lightly oiled silicone mat or greased baking tray and leave it to cool.

When the edges of the syrup begin to firm, fold them in toward the centre with an oiled spatula. Repeat until the mass is cool enough to handle, it should feel warm but not burning when you press the back of a knuckle to the surface, around 60°C. Oil your hands and begin pulling the sugar: stretch it out to about 30 cm, fold it back on itself, twist, and repeat. The candy will change from glassy and sticky to opaque and satiny after 10 to 15 pulls. Work quickly; once it becomes too stiff to stretch, it cannot be worked further.

Roll the pulled candy into a rope about 1.5 cm thick. Cut into 5 cm sticks with oiled scissors. Dust generously with icing sugar to prevent sticking and lay on a parchment-lined tray. Leave uncovered at room temperature overnight. By morning, the sticks will have become soft and powdery, this is the crystallisation process completing. Store in a tin dusted with icing sugar.
